title: Chapter 23. Of the Public Ministers of Sovereign Power
paragraphs: In the last chapter I spoke of the similar parts of a commonwealth; in this I shall speak of the organic parts — namely, the public ministers.

A PUBLIC MINISTER is one who, by the sovereign (whether a monarch or an assembly), is employed in any affair with authority to represent in that employment the person of the commonwealth. Now since every man, or assembly, that has sovereignty represents two persons — or (as it is more commonly put) has two capacities, one natural and one political — a monarch having the person not only of the commonwealth but also of a man, and a sovereign assembly having the person not only of the commonwealth but also of the assembly — those who serve them in their natural capacity are not public ministers; only those who serve them in the administration of the public business are. So neither ushers, nor sergeants, nor any other officers who wait on the assembly for no other purpose than the convenience of the men assembled, in an aristocracy or a democracy, nor stewards, chamberlains, cofferers, nor any other officers of a monarch's household, are public ministers in a monarchy.

Of public ministers, some have charge committed to them of a general administration, either of the whole dominion or of a part of it. Of the whole: as when a Protector or Regent may be entrusted by the predecessor of an infant king, during his minority, with the whole administration of his kingdom. In that case, every subject is obliged to obedience so far as the ordinances the Protector makes, and the commands he gives, are in the king's name and not inconsistent with his sovereign power. Of a part, or province: as when either a monarch or a sovereign assembly gives the general charge of it to a governor, lieutenant, prefect, or viceroy. In this case too, every member of that province is obliged to all that the deputy shall do in the name of the sovereign, provided it is not incompatible with the sovereign's right. For such Protectors, viceroys, and governors have no right except what depends on the sovereign's will; and no commission given to them can be interpreted as a declaration of his will to transfer the sovereignty unless that intention is in express and clear words. This kind of public minister resembles the nerves and tendons that move the various limbs of a natural body.

Others have a special administration — that is, charge of some particular business, either at home or abroad. At home, first, for the economy of the commonwealth: those who have authority over the public treasure — tributes, impositions, rents, fines, or any other public revenue — to collect, receive, disburse, or audit it, are public ministers. Ministers, because they serve the representative person and can do nothing against his command, or without his authority; public, because they serve him in his political capacity.

Second, those who have authority over the militia — to have custody of arms, forts, and ports; to levy, pay, or lead soldiers; or to provide anything necessary for the conduct of war by land or sea — are public ministers. But a soldier without command, though he fights for the commonwealth, does not for that reason represent its person, because there is no one for him to represent it to. Everyone with a command represents the commonwealth only to those whom he commands.

Those also who have authority to teach, or to enable others to teach, the people their duty to the sovereign power, and to instruct them in the knowledge of what is just and unjust — thereby fitting them better to live in godliness and in peace among themselves, and to resist the public enemy — are public ministers. Ministers, in that they do this not by their own authority but by another's; and public, because they do it (or should do it) by no authority but the sovereign's. The monarch, or the sovereign assembly, alone has direct authority from God to teach and instruct the people; and no one but the sovereign receives his power Dei Gratia in the simple sense — that is, from the favour of God alone. All others receive theirs from the favour and providence of God and of their sovereign: in a monarchy, Dei Gratia et Regis, or Dei Providentia et Voluntate Regis.

Those also to whom jurisdiction is given are public ministers. For in their seats of justice they represent the person of the sovereign, and their sentence is his sentence. For (as was declared before) all judicature is essentially annexed to the sovereignty, and so all other judges are only ministers of him, or them, who holds the sovereign power. And as controversies are of two sorts — namely, of fact and of law — so are judgements: some of fact, some of law. So in the same controversy there may be two judges, one of fact, the other of law.

In both these kinds of controversy, a further controversy may arise between the party being judged and the judge himself; and because they are both subjects to the sovereign, this should in equity be judged by men agreed on by the consent of both — for no man can be a judge in his own case. But the sovereign is already agreed on as judge by them both, and so is either to hear the case and decide it himself, or to appoint as judges such men as they both agree on. And this agreement is understood to be made between them in various ways. First, if the defendant is allowed to challenge those of his judges whose interest makes him suspect them (since the complainant has already chosen his own judge), then those he does not challenge are judges he himself agrees on. Second, if he appeals to any other judge, he can appeal no further; his appeal is his choice. Third, if he appeals to the sovereign himself, and the sovereign — either in person, or by delegates the parties shall agree on — gives sentence, that sentence is final; for the defendant is judged by his own judges, that is, by himself.

Considering these properties of just and rational judicature, I cannot help observing the excellent constitution of the courts of justice established in England both for Common Pleas and for Public Pleas. By Common Pleas I mean those in which both the complainant and the defendant are subjects; and by Public Pleas (which are also called Pleas of the Crown) those in which the complainant is the sovereign. Whereas there were two orders of men, one being lords and the other commons, the lords had the privilege of having for their judges in all capital crimes none but lords, and as many of them as would be present — which, being always acknowledged as a privilege of favour, meant their judges were none but those they themselves had wanted. In all controversies, every subject (and likewise the lords in civil controversies) had as judges men of the county where the matter in dispute lay; against whom he could make his challenges, until at last twelve men without challenge were agreed on, and he was judged by those twelve. So having his own judges, the party could allege nothing to keep the sentence from being final. These public persons, with authority from the sovereign power either to instruct or to judge the people, are members of the commonwealth that may fitly be compared to the organs of voice in a natural body.

Public ministers are also all those who have authority from the sovereign to procure the execution of judgements given, to publish the sovereign's commands, to suppress tumults, to apprehend and imprison wrongdoers, and to perform other acts tending to the preservation of peace. For every act they do by such authority is the act of the commonwealth; and their service answers to that of the hands in a natural body.

Public ministers abroad are those who represent the person of their own sovereign to foreign states. Such are ambassadors, messengers, agents, and heralds, sent by public authority and on public business.

But those who are sent by the authority only of some private party of a troubled state, though they are received, are neither public nor private ministers of the commonwealth, because none of their actions have the commonwealth for their author. Likewise, an ambassador sent from a prince to congratulate, condole with, or attend a ceremony — though the authority is public, since the business is private, belonging to the prince in his natural capacity — is a private person. Also if a man is sent into another country to explore their counsels and strength in secret, though both the authority and the business are public, since there is no person in him to be acknowledged but his own, he is only a private minister; but a minister of the commonwealth still, and may be compared to an eye in the natural body. And those who are appointed to receive the petitions or other information of the people, and are as it were the public ear, are public ministers, and represent their sovereign in that office.

Neither a counsellor, nor a council of state, if we consider it as having no authority of judicature or command, but only of giving advice to the sovereign when it is requested, or of offering it unrequested, is a public person. For the advice is addressed to the sovereign alone, whose person cannot in his own presence be represented to him by another. But a body of counsellors is never without some other authority, either of judicature or of immediate administration. In a monarchy, they represent the monarch in delivering his commands to the public ministers. In a democracy, the council, or senate, sets the result of its deliberations before the people as a council; but when it appoints judges, hears cases, or gives audience to ambassadors, it acts in the capacity of a minister of the people. In an aristocracy, the council of state is the sovereign assembly itself, and gives counsel to no one but themselves.
